note: Health-Body lesson, content v3 (136 words). Meanings, lesson sentences and links come from the vocabulary analysis; gaps, hints, common mistakes, collocations, word family, synonyms/antonyms, register and most levels were written for this file. Also 5 grammar rules (be about to, going to, past simple, so that + can/could, verbs + -ing), each with choose / judge / fix questions. Each word and grammar rule lists its course unit(s) in "units" (from the Anki tags).

words.meaning: Good at sports or enjoying physical activity.
situations: He is very athletic because he plays soccer and runs every single morning.
gaps: My sister is very ______ — she swims, plays tennis, and never gets tired.
He was the most ______ student in his class — the best at running, jumping and football.
hints: Describes someone who is strong, fit, and good at sports.
Starts with 'ath-' and ends with '-ic'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He is a very athlete person.
commonMistakes.correction: He is a very athletic person.
commonMistakes.why: 'Athlete' is a noun (the person); use the adjective 'athletic' to describe someone.

words.meaning: A very large amount of something (informal).
situations: I have a ton of homework to finish before the weekend starts.
gaps: There was a ______ of food at the party, so we took some home.
I've got a ______ of emails to answer this morning.
hints: An informal way to say 'a lot', as in 'a ___ of'.
A three-letter word that is also a unit of weight.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have a tons of work today.
commonMistakes.correction: I have tons of work today.
commonMistakes.why: Say 'a ton of' or 'tons of', not 'a tons of'.

words.meaning: So enjoyable that it makes you want to keep doing or using it.
situations: This new puzzle game is so addicting that I can't stop playing it!
gaps: Watching one more episode is so ______ — I always say 'just one more'.
Social media can be very ______, so I turn off my phone at night.
hints: Describes something so fun that you can't stop doing it.
Starts with 'add-' and ends with '-ing'.

commonMistakes.sentence: This game is very addicted.
commonMistakes.correction: This game is very addicting.
commonMistakes.why: 'Addicted' describes the person; 'addicting' (or 'addictive') describes the thing.

words.meaning: Occasionally, but not regularly.
situations: I like to go for a walk in the park from time to time to relax.
gaps: We still meet for coffee ______, but not every week.
______, I forget my keys and have to go back home.
hints: Means 'sometimes, but not often'.
A four-word phrase: from ___ to ___.

commonMistakes.sentence: I visit my grandparents time to time.
commonMistakes.correction: I visit my grandparents from time to time.
commonMistakes.why: The fixed phrase needs 'from': from time to time.

collocations: see someone from time to time

words.meaning: Thinking about someone or something so much that it takes much of your attention.
situations: My little sister is completely obsessed with dinosaurs; she knows every name by heart.
gaps: He is ______ with his new phone and checks it every few minutes.
My brother is ______ with football; it's all he talks about.
hints: Thinking about one thing far too much.
Starts with 'obs-' and ends with '-ed'.

commonMistakes.sentence: She is obsessed about K-pop.
commonMistakes.correction: She is obsessed with K-pop.
commonMistakes.why: We say 'obsessed with', not 'obsessed about'.

words.meaning: Games near the end of a sports competition that help decide the final winner.
situations: My favorite team played so well this year that they finally made it to the playoffs.
gaps: Only the top eight teams make it to the ______ at the end of the season.
They lost the first game of the ______ and were out of the competition.
hints: The final games that decide the champion.
Starts with 'pla-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: We made it to the playoff.
commonMistakes.correction: We made it to the playoffs.
commonMistakes.why: This stage of a competition is usually plural: the playoffs.

words.meaning: Many times; often used without an exact count.
situations: I have watched my favorite movie dozens of times because it never gets boring.
gaps: I've told you ______ to close the door!
She has read that book ______ and still loves it.
hints: Many, many times, without an exact number.
A three-word phrase; a dozen is twelve.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have called him dozen of times.
commonMistakes.correction: I have called him dozens of times.
commonMistakes.why: Use the plural 'dozens of' when you mean many times.

words.meaning: A treatment or remedy that makes an illness go away.
situations: Scientists are still searching for a cure for diabetes.
gaps: The doctors found a ______, and after a month of treatment the illness was completely gone.
Rest and warm soup are not a real ______, but they help you feel better.
hints: Something that makes an illness go away completely.
A four-letter word that starts with 'c'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Doctors are looking for a cure of cancer.
commonMistakes.correction: Doctors are looking for a cure for cancer.
commonMistakes.why: We say 'a cure for' an illness.

words.meaning: A medical examination to check your general health.
situations: She goes for a full check-up every six months.
gaps: The dentist said my teeth were fine and I should come back in six months for a routine ______.
Once a year the company doctor gives every worker a full ______ to make sure they are healthy.
hints: A routine visit to make sure you are healthy.
A hyphenated word: check-__.

commonMistakes.sentence: I need to check up with my doctor next week.
commonMistakes.correction: I need a check-up with my doctor next week.
commonMistakes.why: 'Check-up' (with a hyphen) is the noun; 'check up on' is a verb.

words.meaning: Changes or problems a person experiences that may show illness.
situations: Fever and a sore throat are common symptoms of the flu.
gaps: Tell the doctor about all your ______, like headaches or tiredness.
A high temperature and a cough are the first ______ of a cold.
hints: What you feel when you are ill, like pain or a cough.
Starts with 'sym-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have symptom of a cold.
commonMistakes.correction: I have symptoms of a cold.
commonMistakes.why: We usually talk about several symptoms, so use the plural.

words.meaning: To become larger, especially after an injury or because of illness.
situations: His ankle started to swell after he fell during the match.
gaps: After the bee sting, her hand started to ______ until it was twice its normal size.
If you stand all day, your feet may ______ and your shoes will feel too tight.
hints: To get bigger, often after an injury.
A five-letter word that rhymes with 'bell'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I hit my ankle and now it is swell.
commonMistakes.correction: I hit my ankle and now it is swollen.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'swollen'; 'swell' is the verb.

words.meaning: A condition in which the body has difficulty controlling blood sugar.
situations: He was diagnosed with diabetes and had to change his diet completely.
gaps: People with ______ need to check their blood sugar every day.
Years of eating too much sugar can lead to ______, and then some people need insulin every day.
hints: An illness where the body can't control blood sugar.
Starts with 'dia-' and ends with '-tes'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He has a diabetes.
commonMistakes.correction: He has diabetes.
commonMistakes.why: 'Diabetes' is uncountable, so don't use 'a'.

words.meaning: A growth of cells that is not cancer.
situations: The doctor told her the tumor was benign, so no surgery was needed.
gaps: Good news: the scan showed a ______, not cancer.
Doctors removed a small ______ from her neck; it wasn't cancer, so she didn't need more treatment.
hints: A growth of cells that is not cancer.
Two words; the first starts with 'ben-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The tumor was benevolent, so she was relieved.
commonMistakes.correction: The tumor was benign, so she was relieved.
commonMistakes.why: 'Benign' describes a tumor that is not cancer; 'benevolent' means kind.

words.meaning: An illness that lasts for a long time.
situations: Diabetes and hypertension are both examples of chronic diseases.
gaps: Asthma is a ______ that many people live with for their whole life.
A ______ like arthritis can last for many years.
hints: An illness that lasts for a long time.
Two words; the first starts with 'chr-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: She has a chronic cold that started yesterday.
commonMistakes.correction: She has an acute cold that started yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: 'Chronic' means lasting a long time; a sudden, short illness is 'acute'.

words.meaning: An immune reaction to something that is harmless to most people.
situations: She has a severe allergy to peanuts and always carries medication.
gaps: My sister has an ______ to cats, so she sneezes when she visits us.
Tell the waiter if you have a food ______ before you order.
hints: When your body reacts badly to something harmless, like pollen.
Starts with 'all-' and ends with '-gy'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have an allergy from nuts.
commonMistakes.correction: I have an allergy to nuts.
commonMistakes.why: We say 'an allergy to' something.

words.meaning: Blood pressure that is too high.
situations: He was told to reduce salt and stress to control his hypertension.
gaps: Too much salt and stress can lead to ______, so doctors check your blood pressure regularly.
People with ______ have blood pressure that is too high, so they should eat less salt.
hints: A medical word for blood pressure that is too high.
Starts with 'hyper-', which means 'too much'.

commonMistakes.sentence: My grandfather has hypotension, so he must eat less salt.
commonMistakes.correction: My grandfather has hypertension, so he must eat less salt.
commonMistakes.why: Hypertension is high blood pressure; hypotension is low blood pressure.

words.meaning: A dark mark under the skin caused by damage to small blood vessels.
situations: She had a bruise on her arm after bumping into the door.
gaps: The ball hit his leg and left a big purple ______.
Put ice on it quickly and the dark blue ______ won't be so big tomorrow.
hints: A dark mark on the skin after you hit something.
Starts with 'bru-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: She bruised on her arm.
commonMistakes.correction: She got a bruise on her arm.
commonMistakes.why: Say 'get a bruise' or 'bruise your arm'; the verb needs an object.

words.meaning: Feeling faint, as if you might lose consciousness.
situations: Every day, when I suddenly wake up, I'm lightheaded.
gaps: I skipped breakfast and felt ______ during the meeting, as if I was going to faint.
Stand up slowly or you might feel ______.
hints: Feeling as if you might faint.
Starts with 'lig-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I feel light head today.
commonMistakes.correction: I feel lightheaded today.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is one word (or hyphenated): lightheaded / light-headed.

words.meaning: Very annoyed by something that has continued or happened repeatedly.
situations: I hate my co-workers — I'm sick and tired of working with them.
gaps: I'm ______ of waiting for the bus every morning.
She was ______ of her neighbour's loud music.
hints: Very annoyed because something keeps happening.
'Sick and ___' — the missing word means 'needing sleep'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I'm tired and sick of this noise.
commonMistakes.correction: I'm sick and tired of this noise.
commonMistakes.why: Binomials have a fixed order: always 'sick and tired'.

words.meaning: Confused about facts or how things fit together.
situations: I was completely mixed up about which appointment was today.
gaps: Sorry, I got ______ and went to the wrong room.
The teacher spoke so fast that I was totally ______.
hints: Confused about what is right or where things go.
Two words: the second is the opposite of 'down'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I mixed up about the dates.
commonMistakes.correction: I got mixed up about the dates.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'be/get mixed up about'; 'mix up' needs an object: I mixed up the dates.

words.meaning: To suddenly become very intense or angry, as a disagreement develops.
situations: The argument blew up when no one could agree on the treatment plan.
gaps: Small problems at work can suddenly ______ into a big angry argument if nobody talks about them.
My dad tends to ______ and start shouting when we come home late.
hints: When an argument suddenly becomes big and angry.
A phrasal verb: 'blow' + the opposite of 'down'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The argument blowed up quickly.
commonMistakes.correction: The argument blew up quickly.
commonMistakes.why: The past of 'blow' is 'blew'.

words.meaning: To become well again after an injury, or to help a wound get better.
situations: The wound took two weeks to heal completely.
gaps: Give your hand some rest so the cut can ______.
Broken bones usually ______ in six to eight weeks.
hints: To become healthy again after an injury.
A four-letter word that sounds like 'heel'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I hurt my heal while running.
commonMistakes.correction: I hurt my heel while running.
commonMistakes.why: 'Heel' is the back of your foot; 'heal' means to get better.

words.meaning: An area of irritated skin with spots or changes in colour.
situations: After three days of intense burning pain on his right side, Khaled developed a blistered rash that his doctor officially diagnosed as shingles.
gaps: The new soap gave me an itchy red ______ on my hands.
If the itchy red ______ on your skin spreads, see a doctor.
hints: Red spots or itchy skin.
A four-letter word that starts with 'r'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have rashes red on my arm.
commonMistakes.correction: I have a red rash on my arm.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'a rash' and put the adjective before the noun.

words.meaning: Something observable or measurable that can show a health problem.
situations: Yellowing of the eyes is a sign of liver problems.
gaps: Losing weight very quickly can be a ______ of a health problem.
Red eyes are often a ______ that you need more sleep.
hints: Something you can see that shows there may be a problem.
A four-letter word with a silent 'g'.

commonMistakes.sentence: A high temperature is a sign for illness.
commonMistakes.correction: A high temperature is a sign of illness.
commonMistakes.why: We say 'a sign of' something.

words.meaning: Larger than usual because of injury, illness, or a build-up of fluid.
situations: His knee was so swollen he couldn't walk after the fall.
gaps: Her eyes were red and ______ after she cried all night.
My fingers get so ______ when it's very hot that my ring won't come off.
hints: Bigger than normal because of an injury or illness.
Starts with 'swo-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: My ankle is swelled.
commonMistakes.correction: My ankle is swollen.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective form is 'swollen', not 'swelled'.

words.meaning: The state of being ill.
situations: His sickness kept him home for an entire week.
gaps: Morning ______ is common for pregnant women in the first months.
Some people get motion ______ when they travel by boat.
hints: The state of being ill.
Starts with 'sic-' and ends with '-ness'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He missed school because of a sick.
commonMistakes.correction: He missed school because of sickness.
commonMistakes.why: 'Sick' is an adjective; the noun is 'sickness'.

words.meaning: A disease or a period or state of poor health.
situations: She recovered from a serious illness after months of treatment.
gaps: She missed three weeks of school because of a long ______ and needed time to get her strength back.
After years of stress, he developed a serious ______ and spent months in hospital.
hints: A period of being unwell.
Starts with 'ill-' and ends with '-ness'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He is suffering from a serious ill.
commonMistakes.correction: He is suffering from a serious illness.
commonMistakes.why: 'Ill' is an adjective; the noun is 'illness'.

words.meaning: A condition that affects the normal working of the body or mind.
situations: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death worldwide.
gaps: Malaria is a dangerous ______ that people can catch from mosquitoes.
Smoking can cause heart ______ and many other health problems.
hints: A condition that stops the body working normally.
Starts with 'dis-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Doctors discovered a new decease.
commonMistakes.correction: Doctors discovered a new disease.
commonMistakes.why: 'Disease' means illness; 'decease' means death.

words.meaning: A cancerous growth that can invade nearby tissue or spread.
situations: The biopsy confirmed the tumor was malignant and required immediate surgery.
gaps: Doctors must act fast when they find a ______ because it can spread.
The tests showed a ______ that could spread to other organs, so she started treatment right away.
hints: A growth of cells that is cancer.
Two words; the first starts with 'mal-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The tumor was malicious, so she needed treatment.
commonMistakes.correction: The tumor was malignant, so she needed treatment.
commonMistakes.why: 'Malignant' is the medical word for cancerous; 'malicious' means wanting to hurt someone.

words.meaning: Having an allergy to a particular substance.
situations: He is allergic to dust, which causes him to sneeze constantly.
gaps: I can't eat this cake because I'm ______ nuts.
Is anyone here ______ cats? I have two at home.
hints: Having a bad body reaction to something.
Starts with 'all-' and ends with 'to'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I'm allergic with seafood.
commonMistakes.correction: I'm allergic to seafood.
commonMistakes.why: The preposition is always 'to': allergic to.

words.meaning: Blood pressure that is too low.
situations: She felt faint because of hypotension after standing up too quickly.
gaps: People with ______ may feel dizzy when they stand up quickly.
Drinking more water and eating a little more salt can help with ______, when blood pressure is too low.
hints: Blood pressure that is too low.
Starts with 'hypo-', which means 'under'.

commonMistakes.sentence: She has hypertension, so she feels faint when she stands.
commonMistakes.correction: She has hypotension, so she feels faint when she stands.
commonMistakes.why: Hypotension is low blood pressure; hypertension is high.

words.meaning: Brain injury caused by blocked blood flow or bleeding in the brain.
situations: He had a stroke at 60 but recovered after months of physiotherapy.
gaps: Sudden weakness on one side of the face can be a sign of a ______.
After his ______, the blood flow to part of his brain was damaged, and he had to learn to speak again.
hints: A sudden brain injury caused by a blocked or broken blood vessel.
A six-letter word; it also means a gentle touch.

commonMistakes.sentence: He got a stroke last year.
commonMistakes.correction: He had a stroke last year.
commonMistakes.why: We usually say 'have a stroke'.

words.meaning: A deep state of unconsciousness in which a person cannot be woken normally.
situations: The patient was in a coma for three days before regaining consciousness.
gaps: After the accident he was in a ______ for three weeks and couldn't wake up.
Doctors put him into a ______ to help his brain rest.
hints: A deep sleep-like state that a person can't wake up from.
A four-letter word that starts with 'c'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He was in coma for a week.
commonMistakes.correction: He was in a coma for a week.
commonMistakes.why: We say 'in a coma', with 'a'.

words.meaning: Small solid pieces of medicine, usually made by pressing powder.
situations: Take two tablets after each meal.
gaps: Take one of these ______ with water every morning.
The ______ are too big, so I break them in half.
hints: Small hard pieces of medicine you swallow.
Starts with 'tab-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I bought a tablets for my headache.
commonMistakes.correction: I bought some tablets for my headache.
commonMistakes.why: 'Tablets' is plural, so don't use 'a'.

words.meaning: Liquid medicine given in very small amounts, often into the eyes, ears, or nose.
situations: The doctor prescribed eye drops to treat the infection.
gaps: Put two ______ in each eye before you go to bed.
The doctor gave me ear ______ for the infection.
hints: Liquid medicine for the eyes, ears, or nose.
Starts with 'dro-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I put some drop in my eyes.
commonMistakes.correction: I put some drops in my eyes.
commonMistakes.why: Eye medicine is usually 'drops' (plural).

words.meaning: The act of putting medicine or another substance into the body with a needle.
situations: The nurse gave him an injection before the operation.
gaps: The nurse will give you an ______ in your arm; it only hurts for a second.
Some children cry when they have to get an ______.
hints: Medicine put into the body with a needle.
Starts with 'inj-' and ends with '-tion'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The nurse made me an injection.
commonMistakes.correction: The nurse gave me an injection.
commonMistakes.why: We say 'give someone an injection' or 'have an injection'.

words.meaning: Small solid medicines taken by mouth, including tablets and capsules in everyday use.
situations: He takes blood pressure pills every morning without fail.
gaps: The doctor told me to take two ______ after breakfast with a glass of water.
Keep all ______ in a high cupboard where children can't reach them.
hints: Small solid medicines that you swallow.
A five-letter word that starts with 'p'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I drank two pills for my headache.
commonMistakes.correction: I took two pills for my headache.
commonMistakes.why: We take or swallow pills; we drink liquids.

words.meaning: Medicines inside small containers that dissolve after being swallowed.
situations: The doctor gave me capsules that I swallow with water twice a day.
gaps: These ______ have powder inside a soft shell.
Swallow the ______ whole; don't open them.
hints: Medicine in a small shell that you swallow.
Starts with 'cap-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Take a capsules every day.
commonMistakes.correction: Take a capsule every day.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'a capsule' for one and 'capsules' for more than one.

words.meaning: A medicine used to reduce pain.
situations: The doctor gave her a painkiller for her headache.
gaps: I took a ______, and my toothache went away.
This ______ stops headaches fast, but it can make you sleepy.
hints: Medicine that makes pain go away.
Starts with 'pai-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I took a painkiller medicine.
commonMistakes.correction: I took a painkiller.
commonMistakes.why: 'Painkiller' already means the medicine.

words.meaning: A thick substance applied to the skin as a treatment or protection.
situations: The doctor prescribed an ointment to treat the rash on her arm.
gaps: Rub this ______ on the burn twice a day.
The ______ helped the dry skin on my hands.
hints: A thick cream you put on your skin as medicine.
Starts with 'oin-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I put a ointment on the cut.
commonMistakes.correction: I put an ointment on the cut.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'an' before a vowel sound.

words.meaning: A hard covering that supports and protects a broken bone while it heals.
situations: He wore a cast on his arm for six weeks after breaking it.
gaps: After she broke her leg, the doctor put it in a ______ for two months.
The children drew funny pictures on her ______ while her leg healed.
hints: A hard cover that keeps a broken bone still while it heals.
A four-letter word that also means all the actors in a film.

commonMistakes.sentence: The doctor put a bandage on his broken arm to keep the bone still for six weeks.
commonMistakes.correction: The doctor put a cast on his broken arm to keep the bone still for six weeks.
commonMistakes.why: A bandage is soft material; the hard cover that holds a broken bone still is a cast.

words.meaning: Not feeling well because of a disease or infection.
situations: She stayed at home because she was sick.
gaps: I had a fever and felt too ______ to go to work, so I stayed in bed.
Grandma was ______ last week, but she's feeling much better now.
hints: How you feel when you have a cold, the flu, or another illness.
A four-letter word that starts with 's'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I feel sickness today, so I'm staying home.
commonMistakes.correction: I feel sick today, so I'm staying home.
commonMistakes.why: 'Sick' is the adjective for how you feel; 'sickness' is the noun.

words.meaning: Having less colour in the skin than usual.
situations: He looked pale after waiting in the hospital all day.
gaps: You look very ______ — are you feeling OK?
Her face went ______ when she saw the blood.
hints: Having less colour in your face than usual.
A four-letter word that starts with 'p'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He looks palely today.
commonMistakes.correction: He looks pale today.
commonMistakes.why: After 'look' meaning 'seem', use an adjective, not an adverb.

words.meaning: A body temperature that is higher than normal.
situations: The child had a fever, so his mother took him to the doctor.
gaps: Drink lots of water when you have a ______ and your temperature is high.
Her ______ went down after she took some medicine.
hints: A body temperature that is higher than normal.
Starts with 'fev-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He has fever of 39 degrees.
commonMistakes.correction: He has a fever of 39 degrees.
commonMistakes.why: We usually say 'a fever' (or 'a temperature').

words.meaning: A person receiving medical care.
situations: The doctor saw ten patients this morning.
gaps: Dr. Ali has already seen every ______ on his list today.
Each ______ gets a bed and a nurse on this floor.
hints: A person who is getting medical care.
Starts with 'pat-'; it also means calm when you wait.

commonMistakes.sentence: The doctor has many clients today.
commonMistakes.correction: The doctor has many patients today.
commonMistakes.why: People who see a doctor are 'patients', not 'clients' or 'customers'.

words.meaning: A strip or piece of material used to cover or support an injured part of the body.
situations: The nurse put a bandage around his injured arm.
gaps: Wrap the ______ around the cut to stop the bleeding.
She changed the ______ on her knee every morning.
hints: A strip of cloth used to cover an injury.
Starts with 'ban-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The doctor put a cast on my small cut.
commonMistakes.correction: The nurse put a bandage on my small cut.
commonMistakes.why: A small cut needs a bandage; a cast is hard and holds a broken bone.

words.meaning: A liquid medicine that is often thick and sweet.
situations: The child took a spoon of cough syrup before bed.
gaps: Take one spoonful of this sweet, thick ______ every four hours.
Children usually like cough ______ because it tastes sweet.
hints: Thick, sweet liquid medicine.
Starts with 'syr-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Eat two spoons of syrup.
commonMistakes.correction: Take two spoonfuls of syrup.
commonMistakes.why: We 'take' medicine, including syrup.

words.meaning: A medical procedure in which a surgeon treats part of the body.
situations: He had an operation to fix his broken knee.
gaps: After the ______ on her stomach, she stayed in hospital for three days.
The surgeon said the ______ went well.
hints: When a surgeon cuts into the body to treat it.
Starts with 'ope-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He made an operation on his heart.
commonMistakes.correction: He had an operation on his heart.
commonMistakes.why: The patient 'has' an operation; the surgeon 'performs' it.

words.meaning: To suddenly force air out through the nose and mouth.
situations: She sneezed three times during the class.
gaps: Pepper always makes me ______ — achoo!
Dust always gets up my nose and makes me ______.
hints: What you do suddenly through your nose — 'achoo!'.
Starts with 'sne-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He did a sneeze very loud.
commonMistakes.correction: He sneezed very loudly.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'sneeze' as a verb, and 'loudly' (an adverb) to say how.

words.meaning: To look at or check someone carefully, especially during a medical examination.
situations: The doctor examined the patient and wrote a prescription.
gaps: The doctor needs to ______ your throat.
A nurse will ______ you before the operation.
hints: To look at someone carefully to check their health.
Starts with 'exa-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The doctor examined to my ears.
commonMistakes.correction: The doctor examined my ears.
commonMistakes.why: 'Examine' takes a direct object, with no 'to'.

words.meaning: Feeling unsteady or as if you or your surroundings are spinning.
situations: She felt dizzy after standing up too quickly.

The smell of the barbecue made the dog ______.
hints: To let liquid come out of your mouth, like a baby.
A five-letter word with a double 'o'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He drooled his saliva on the pillow.
commonMistakes.correction: He drooled on the pillow.
commonMistakes.why: 'Drool' already means letting saliva out.

words.meaning: The act or sound of breathing noisily while asleep.
situations: My father's snoring was so loud that nobody in the house could sleep.
gaps: Sleeping on your back can make ______ worse.
His ______ got better after he lost some weight.
hints: The noisy breathing some people make while they sleep.
Starts with 'sno-' and ends with '-ing'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He makes snore every night.
commonMistakes.correction: He snores every night.
commonMistakes.why: Use the verb 'snore'; 'snoring' is the noun.

words.meaning: To remain awake instead of going to bed.
situations: I stayed up until 3 AM watching a series and regretted it the next morning.
gaps: Kids are allowed to ______ late on Friday nights to watch a movie.
Don't ______ too late; you have an exam tomorrow.
hints: To not go to bed at your usual time.
A phrasal verb: 'stay' + the opposite of 'down'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I woke up until midnight to finish my homework.
commonMistakes.correction: I stayed up until midnight to finish my homework.
commonMistakes.why: 'Wake up' means to stop sleeping; 'stay up' means to not go to bed.

words.meaning: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting enough sleep.
situations: She has been suffering from insomnia for months and feels exhausted every day.
gaps: Drinking coffee late at night can cause ______.
Because of her ______, she reads until 4 a.m. most nights.
hints: When you can't sleep, night after night.
Starts with 'ins-' and ends with '-ia'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have insomnias.
commonMistakes.correction: I have insomnia.
commonMistakes.why: 'Insomnia' is uncountable.

words.meaning: Existing in the mind without being fully noticed or consciously controlled.
situations: Many psychologists believe that dreams come from the subconscious mind.
gaps: Some of our fears come from ______ memories from childhood.
Biting his nails was a ______ habit; he didn't notice he was doing it.
hints: In your mind, but not fully noticed by you.
Starts with 'sub-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He was subconscious after the accident.
commonMistakes.correction: He was unconscious after the accident.
commonMistakes.why: 'Unconscious' means not awake; 'subconscious' is about hidden thoughts.

words.meaning: A condition that affects normal sleep.
situations: Insomnia and sleep apnea are two of the most common sleep disorders.
gaps: Snoring very loudly can be a sign of a ______.
If you are always tired, you may have a ______.
hints: A health problem that affects how you sleep.
Two words; the second starts with 'dis-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: She has a sleeping disorder.
commonMistakes.correction: She has a sleep disorder.
commonMistakes.why: The usual term is 'sleep disorder'.

words.meaning: To imagine pleasant things while awake instead of paying attention.
situations: I was daydreaming about my next holiday instead of paying attention in the meeting.
gaps: Stop looking out of the window — don't ______ in class!
I love to ______ about living by the sea.
hints: To think about nice things while you are awake.
Starts with 'day-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I was day dreaming in the meeting.
commonMistakes.correction: I was daydreaming in the meeting.
commonMistakes.why: 'Daydream' is one word.

words.meaning: An occasion when someone, especially a child, stays overnight at a friend's home.
situations: My daughter is so excited about her first sleepover at her best friend's house.
gaps: Five girls came to our house for a birthday ______ and slept on the living room floor.
The kids watched movies all night at the ______ and stayed until the next morning.
hints: A night when kids stay at a friend's house.
Starts with 'sle-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: We did a sleep over at my house.
commonMistakes.correction: We had a sleepover at my house.
commonMistakes.why: 'Sleepover' is one word, and we usually 'have' one.

words.meaning: An explanation or understanding of what something means.
situations: There are many different interpretations of what it means to dream about water.
gaps: Each student gave a different ______ of the poem.
Her ______ of the results was very clear.
hints: An explanation of what something means.
Starts with 'int-' and ends with '-tion'.

commonMistakes.sentence: What is your interpret of the story?
commonMistakes.correction: What is your interpretation of the story?
commonMistakes.why: 'Interpret' is the verb; the noun is 'interpretation'.

words.meaning: A frightening or upsetting dream while asleep.
situations: She woke up screaming after having a nightmare about being trapped in a dark room.
gaps: After watching the horror film, he had a ______ about zombies.
My little brother woke up crying from a bad ______.
hints: A very scary dream.
Starts with 'nig-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I dreamed a nightmare.
commonMistakes.correction: I had a nightmare.
commonMistakes.why: We say 'have a nightmare'.

words.meaning: The liquid naturally produced in the mouth.
situations: Saliva production increases when you smell or see food you like.
gaps: Your mouth makes more ______ when you're hungry.
Doctors can test your ______ for some illnesses.
hints: The liquid in your mouth.
Starts with 'sal-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have too many saliva.
commonMistakes.correction: I have too much saliva.
commonMistakes.why: 'Saliva' is uncountable, so use 'much'.

words.meaning: A brief inability to move or speak while falling asleep or waking up.
situations: He experienced sleep paralysis and felt like something was pressing on his chest.
gaps: During ______, you are awake but you can't move your body.
Stress and too little rest can make ______ happen more often.
hints: A short time when you wake up but can't move.
Two words; the second starts with 'par-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I had a sleep paralyse last night.
commonMistakes.correction: I had sleep paralysis last night.
commonMistakes.why: The noun is 'paralysis' (the verb is 'paralyse' / 'paralyze').

words.meaning: Walking or doing other activities while still asleep.
situations: His parents were worried when they discovered he had been sleepwalking every night.
gaps: Doctors say you shouldn't suddenly wake someone who is ______.
______ is more common in children than in adults.
hints: Walking around while you are still asleep.
Starts with 'sle-' and ends with '-ing'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He walks sleeping at night.
commonMistakes.correction: He sleepwalks at night.
commonMistakes.why: The verb is 'sleepwalk'; the noun is 'sleepwalking'.

words.meaning: Speaking while asleep.
situations: My roommate scared me last night — he was sleep talking and saying strange things.
gaps: My wife says I was ______ in Arabic last night.
______ is usually harmless, but it can wake up other people.
hints: Speaking while you are asleep.
Two words; the second ends with '-ing'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He was talking sleep last night.
commonMistakes.correction: He was sleep talking last night.
commonMistakes.why: The order is 'sleep talking'.

words.meaning: To stop paying attention to what is happening around you; informal.
situations: I zoned out completely during the lecture and missed everything the teacher said.
gaps: It's easy to ______ when a meeting goes on for two hours.
Sorry, I started to ______ — can you repeat that?
hints: To stop paying attention (informal).
A phrasal verb: 'zone' + the opposite of 'in'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I zoned off during the class.
commonMistakes.correction: I zoned out during the class.
commonMistakes.why: The phrasal verb is 'zone out'.

words.meaning: To get some sleep; informal.
situations: I worked all day — I really need to catch some Z's.
gaps: I'm going to ______ before the night shift starts.
You look exhausted — go home and ______.
hints: An informal way to say 'get some sleep'.
Three words; the last one is the letter comics use for sleeping.

commonMistakes.sentence: I need to catch some Z.
commonMistakes.correction: I need to catch some Z's.
commonMistakes.why: The idiom uses the plural: Z's.

words.meaning: Moving around repeatedly in bed because you cannot settle or sleep comfortably.
situations: I had an important meeting the next day — I kept tossing and turning all night.
gaps: The room was so hot that I was ______ until 3 a.m.
He spent the night ______, worrying about his exam.
hints: Moving a lot in bed because you can't sleep.
'Tossing and ___' — the missing word also means changing direction.

commonMistakes.sentence: I was turning and tossing all night.
commonMistakes.correction: I was tossing and turning all night.
commonMistakes.why: Binomials have a fixed order: tossing and turning.

words.word: Your guess is as good as mine
words.meaning: I do not know the answer any more than you do.
situations: A: Why did he quit his job? B: IDK — your guess is as good as mine.
gaps: A: When will the train arrive? B: ______ — there's no information.
A: What's in the box? B: ______!
hints: A friendly way to say 'I don't know either'.
Seven words; it starts with 'Your'.

commonMistakes.sentence: Your guess is good like mine.
commonMistakes.correction: Your guess is as good as mine.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'as good as' to compare.

words.meaning: To compensate for a loss, problem, or missing thing.
situations: I missed the gym yesterday, so I'll make up for it with a longer session today.
gaps: He bought her flowers to ______ forgetting her birthday.
Nothing can ______ the time we lost.
hints: To do something good because of something bad or missing.
A three-word phrasal verb: make ___ ___.

commonMistakes.sentence: I'll make up it for you.
commonMistakes.correction: I'll make up for it.
commonMistakes.why: Say 'make up for something' (or 'make it up to someone').

words.meaning: To force air out of the lungs suddenly, often with a sharp sound.
situations: He has been coughing all night because of his cold.
gaps: The thick smoke got into our throats and made everyone ______.
If you ______ for more than three weeks, see a doctor.
hints: To push air out of your throat with a loud sound.
A five-letter word; the 'gh' sounds like 'f'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He coughed a lot because of cold.
commonMistakes.correction: He coughed a lot because of his cold.
commonMistakes.why: Use a word like 'his' or 'a' before 'cold' when it means the illness.

words.meaning: An arm with a fractured bone.
situations: He fell off his bike and ended up with a broken arm.
gaps: She can't write this week because she has a ______.
A ______ usually needs a cast for about six weeks.
hints: An arm with a bone that is broken.
Two words; the second is a body part.

commonMistakes.sentence: He has a break arm.
commonMistakes.correction: He has a broken arm.
commonMistakes.why: Use the adjective 'broken' before the noun.

words.meaning: An arrangement to meet someone at a particular time.
situations: I have a doctor's appointment tomorrow morning.
gaps: I'm sorry I'm late for our ______ — the doctor was waiting for me.
My dentist ______ is at 3 o'clock on Friday.
hints: A planned time to meet someone, like a doctor.
Starts with 'app-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have a date with the doctor at 10.
commonMistakes.correction: I have an appointment with the doctor at 10.
commonMistakes.why: A meeting with a doctor is an 'appointment'; a 'date' is romantic.

words.meaning: Medical treatment performed by operating on the body.
situations: He needs surgery to fix his broken knee.
gaps: She had ______ on her eyes and now she doesn't need glasses.
Recovery after heart ______ can take months.
hints: Medical treatment where a doctor cuts into the body.
Starts with 'sur-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He had a surgery yesterday.
commonMistakes.correction: He had surgery yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: In this meaning, 'surgery' is usually uncountable.

words.meaning: A nose from which liquid mucus is coming out.
situations: He has a runny nose and keeps sneezing all day.
gaps: Take some tissues — you have a ______.
A ______ is often the first sign of a cold.
hints: When liquid keeps coming out of your nose.
Two words; the first rhymes with 'funny'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have a running nose.
commonMistakes.correction: I have a runny nose.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'runny', not 'running'.

words.meaning: A nose that feels blocked and is difficult to breathe through.
situations: I have a stuffy nose because of my allergies.
gaps: I can't smell anything because of my ______.
A hot shower can help a ______.
hints: When your nose feels blocked.
Two words; the first starts with 'stu-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: My nose is stuffing.
commonMistakes.correction: My nose is stuffy.
commonMistakes.why: Use the adjective 'stuffy'.

words.meaning: To move food, drink, or another substance from the mouth down the throat.
situations: It hurts when I swallow because my throat is so sore.
gaps: Chew your food well before you ______.
The pill is too big — I can't ______ it.
hints: To move food or drink down your throat.
Starts with 'swa-'; it's also the name of a bird.

commonMistakes.sentence: It hurts when I swallowing.
commonMistakes.correction: It hurts when I swallow.
commonMistakes.why: After 'when I', use the simple form of the verb.

words.meaning: Pain or irritation in the throat.
situations: I have a sore throat, so I've been drinking warm tea all day.
gaps: Singing for three hours gave me a ______.
A ______ makes it hard to swallow.
hints: Pain in your throat, often with a cold.
Two words; the first rhymes with 'more'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I have a sour throat.
commonMistakes.correction: I have a sore throat.
commonMistakes.why: 'Sore' means painful; 'sour' is a taste.

words.meaning: To cover or surround something with material.
situations: The nurse wrapped his ankle with a bandage.
gaps: Please ______ the present in the red paper.
______ the baby in a warm blanket before you go outside.
hints: To cover something with paper or cloth.
A four-letter word with a silent 'w'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I wrapped a bandage his arm.
commonMistakes.correction: I wrapped a bandage around his arm.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'wrap something around something'.

words.meaning: Having or feeling as if you have a fever.
situations: He felt feverish and had to stay in bed all day.
gaps: The little boy felt hot and ______, so his mom took his temperature.
I felt ______ all night and couldn't sleep.
hints: Feeling hot because you have a fever.
Starts with 'fev-' and ends with '-ish'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I feel fever today.
commonMistakes.correction: I feel feverish today.
commonMistakes.why: After 'feel', use the adjective 'feverish' (or say 'I have a fever').

words.meaning: Thin hollow instruments used to inject substances into the body or draw fluid out.
situations: She is afraid of needles and always gets nervous before an injection.
gaps: My little brother cries every time he sees the doctor's ______.
Nurses throw used ______ into a special box.
hints: Thin, sharp tools used for injections.
Starts with 'nee-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I'm scared of needle.
commonMistakes.correction: I'm scared of needles.
commonMistakes.why: When you talk about them in general, use the plural: needles.

words.meaning: To arrange a meeting or visit for a particular time.
situations: I need to book an appointment with my dentist for next week.
gaps: Call the clinic to ______ for next Tuesday.
You can ______ online on the hospital's website.
hints: To arrange a time to see a doctor or dentist.
Three words; the first is also something you read.

commonMistakes.sentence: I need to book a date with the dentist.
commonMistakes.correction: I need to book an appointment with the dentist.
commonMistakes.why: With doctors and dentists, we book an 'appointment'.

words.meaning: To supply the medicine that a doctor has ordered on a prescription.
situations: The pharmacist can fill a prescription in about ten minutes.
gaps: The pharmacist will ______ while you wait.
Take this paper to any pharmacy, and they will ______ for you.
hints: What a pharmacist does when they give you the medicine your doctor ordered.
Three words; the first is the opposite of 'empty'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I need to fill in my prescription at the pharmacy.
commonMistakes.correction: I need to get my prescription filled at the pharmacy.
commonMistakes.why: 'Fill in' is for forms; a pharmacy 'fills' a prescription.

grammar.rule: Be about to (something happens very soon)
grammar.explanation: Use am/is/are + about to + base verb for something that will happen in a moment. For plans days or weeks away, use going to.
examples: My last exam is tomorrow — I'm about to graduate.
Her wedding starts in ten minutes — she's about to get married.
Are you about to finish the course?

commonMistakes.sentence: I'm about to travel next month.
commonMistakes.correction: I'm going to travel next month.
commonMistakes.why: About to means in a moment, not weeks away.

commonMistakes.sentence: She is about to leaving.
commonMistakes.correction: She is about to leave.
commonMistakes.why: After about to, use the base verb.

questions.prompt: The nurse has the needle ready. She ______ give you the injection.
questions.answer: is about to
questions.explanation: am/is/are + about to + base verb: it will happen in a moment.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is about something that will happen in a moment?
options: The patient is about to wake up.
The patient woke up at six.
The patient wakes up early every day.
questions.answer: The patient is about to wake up.
questions.explanation: About to = very soon, in a moment.

questions.sentence: I'm about to see the dentist next month.
questions.fix: I'm going to see the dentist next month.
questions.explanation: Next month is not in a moment, so use going to for the plan.

questions.sentence: Hurry! The pharmacy is about to close.
questions.alternative: Hurry! The pharmacy is about closing.
questions.explanation: It will close in a moment: is about to + base verb.

questions.sentence: He is about to fainting.
questions.answer: He is about to faint.
questions.explanation: After about to, use the base verb: faint.

questions.sentence: Are you about leave the hospital?
questions.answer: Are you about to leave the hospital?
questions.explanation: Don't drop to: about to + base verb.

grammar.explanation: Use am/is/are + going to + base verb for plans you decided before speaking, and for predictions from what you can see now. Negative: isn't/aren't going to. Question: Are you going to…?
examples: I'm going to travel to the UAE in 3 days.
Are you going to leave the country?
He isn't going to hang out with me.
Look at those dark clouds — it's going to rain.

commonMistakes.sentence: I going to see a doctor.
commonMistakes.correction: I'm going to see a doctor.
commonMistakes.why: Don't forget am/is/are before going to.

commonMistakes.sentence: She is going to visits her aunt.
commonMistakes.correction: She is going to visit her aunt.
commonMistakes.why: After going to, use the base verb.

questions.prompt: I've booked an appointment. I ______ see the doctor on Monday.
questions.answer: am going to
questions.explanation: A plan decided before speaking: am/is/are + going to + base verb.

questions.prompt: Look at his face! He ______ be sick.
questions.answer: is going to
questions.explanation: A prediction from what you can see now: is going to.

questions.sentence: She not going to join the gym.
questions.fix: She isn't going to join the gym.
questions.explanation: The negative needs is: isn't going to.

questions.sentence: Are you going to take the medicine tonight?
questions.alternative: Are you going to taking the medicine tonight?
questions.explanation: After going to, use the base verb: take.

questions.sentence: We are going to starting a diet next week.
questions.answer: We are going to start a diet next week.
questions.explanation: After going to, use the base verb: start.

questions.sentence: They going to visit their grandmother in hospital.
questions.answer: They are going to visit their grandmother in hospital.
questions.explanation: Don't forget are before going to.

grammar.explanation: Use the past simple for finished actions at a specific past time (yesterday, last week, 10 years ago). Regular verbs add -ed (play → played); irregular verbs have their own form (go → went, wake → woke). Use was/were for past states. After didn't, use the base verb.
examples: They woke up late this morning.
We were excited. He was sick yesterday.
I was a student 10 years ago.

commonMistakes.sentence: I goed to the doctor yesterday.
commonMistakes.correction: I went to the doctor yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: Go is irregular: go → went.

commonMistakes.sentence: We was tired after the match.
commonMistakes.correction: We were tired after the match.
commonMistakes.why: Use were with we, you and they.

questions.prompt: Yesterday I ______ my ankle playing football.
questions.answer: hurt
questions.explanation: Hurt is irregular: its past form is also hurt.

questions.prompt: She ______ sick last week, so she stayed at home.
questions.answer: was
questions.explanation: A past state with she: was.

questions.sentence: He breaked his arm last year.
questions.fix: He broke his arm last year.
questions.explanation: Break is irregular: break → broke.

questions.sentence: We were at the hospital all night.
questions.alternative: We was at the hospital all night.
questions.explanation: With we, the past of be is were.

questions.sentence: I wake up with a headache yesterday.
questions.answer: I woke up with a headache yesterday.
questions.explanation: Yesterday is finished time: wake → woke.

questions.sentence: They didn't went to the gym yesterday.
questions.answer: They didn't go to the gym yesterday.
questions.explanation: After didn't, use the base verb: go.

grammar.explanation: Use so that to give the purpose of an action. So that + can is common for a present or future purpose; so that + could for a past purpose. After can/could, use the base verb.
examples: I drink coffee so that I can focus.
I took this course so that I could find a job.
I slept early so that I could wake up early.

commonMistakes.sentence: I slept early so that I can wake up early.
commonMistakes.correction: I slept early so that I could wake up early.
commonMistakes.why: The action is in the past, so use could.

commonMistakes.sentence: I exercise so that I can to stay fit.
commonMistakes.correction: I exercise so that I can stay fit.
commonMistakes.why: After can/could, use the base verb without to.

questions.prompt: I went to bed early last night so that I ______ rest.
questions.answer: could
questions.explanation: A past action (went) → so that + could + base verb.

questions.prompt: I walk every day so that I ______ stay healthy.
questions.answer: can
questions.explanation: A present habit → so that + can + base verb.

questions.sentence: She took the painkiller so that she can sleep.
questions.fix: She took the painkiller so that she could sleep.
questions.explanation: Took is past, so the purpose uses could.

questions.sentence: I eat vegetables so that I can stay strong.
questions.alternative: I eat vegetables so that I could stay strong.
questions.explanation: Eat is present, so the purpose uses can.

questions.sentence: I stretched before the race so that I can run faster.
questions.answer: I stretched before the race so that I could run faster.
questions.explanation: Stretched is past, so use could.

questions.sentence: I drink water so that I can to stay hydrated.
questions.answer: I drink water so that I can stay hydrated.
questions.explanation: After can, use the base verb without to.

grammar.rule: Verbs followed by -ing (enjoy, keep, quit, don't mind…)
grammar.explanation: When a verb comes after enjoy, keep, quit or don't mind (also finish, avoid, consider, suggest, practise), use the -ing form.
examples: I quit studying at the university.
I don't mind travelling to Alex.

commonMistakes.sentence: I enjoy to swim.
commonMistakes.correction: I enjoy swimming.
commonMistakes.why: Enjoy is followed by -ing, not to.

commonMistakes.sentence: You should avoid to eat too much sugar.
commonMistakes.correction: You should avoid eating too much sugar.
commonMistakes.why: Avoid is followed by -ing.

questions.prompt: My father quit ______ ten years ago.
questions.answer: smoking
questions.explanation: Quit + -ing.

questions.answer: drinking
questions.explanation: Suggest + -ing.

questions.sentence: I don't mind to wait for the doctor.
questions.fix: I don't mind waiting for the doctor.
questions.explanation: Don't mind + -ing.

questions.sentence: She keeps coughing at night.
questions.alternative: She keeps to cough at night.
questions.explanation: Keep + -ing.

questions.sentence: You should avoid to lift heavy boxes.
questions.answer: You should avoid lifting heavy boxes.
questions.explanation: Avoid + -ing.

questions.sentence: Have you finished to take the antibiotics?
questions.answer: Have you finished taking the antibiotics?
questions.explanation: Finish + -ing.
